title: Read the Feed Like a Contract
subtitle: The numbers the brief will cite arrive with quirks
scenario: It is 6:18 AM. The intake record exists - the 2 AM ERCOT spike is on the books as structured fields. Now the numbers the brief will actually cite arrive from a second, independent source: the nightly price file. It corroborates the note ($187 peak, $142 settle), but it promises columns, not cleanliness. Read it like a contract before anyone computes on it.
input:
hub, peak, settled
ercot, $187/MWh, $142/MWh
SPP, $96/MWh, $88/MWh
miso, $74 /MWh, $70/MWh

Delivery: dropped nightly by the market data export, expected before 6:15 AM.
instructions: Read the header row, then read each data row slowly - the quirks are the lesson.
Tag the contract, the case's number, the two quirks, and the schedule to their exact spans.
Validate to record the feed profile.

segments.text: dropped nightly by the market data export

fields.label: The contract (column promise)
fields.explain: The contract is the header row: hub, peak, settled - the producer's promise about every future file. Data cells are instances of the promise, not the promise itself.

fields.label: Today's ERCOT peak
fields.explain: The feed corroborates the note: the flagged hub's peak is $187/MWh. Same number, second source - that agreement is what lets the brief cite it.

fields.label: Casing quirk
fields.explain: Compare the hub cells: SPP arrived uppercase the way a hub code should; 'ercot' arrived lowercase. The quirk is the cell that drifted, not the one that behaved.

fields.label: Spacing quirk
fields.explain: Look character by character: '$74 /MWh' carries a stray space before the unit. A parser written for '$96/MWh' chokes on exactly this kind of drift.

fields.label: Delivery schedule
fields.explain: Who drops the file is provenance; WHEN it is due is the schedule. Everything downstream inherits 'before 6:15 AM' - a late feed is a late brief.

intro.heading: Before you tag: feeds are promises

sections.title: A header row is a contract
sections.body: hub, peak, settled is not just a label line - it is the producer's promise about every future file: these columns, this order. Pipelines are built against that promise.

sections.title: Contracts have gaps
sections.body: The contract says which columns arrive. It says nothing about casing, spacing, or units - and today's file drifts on all three. Reading one real file closely tells you what the contract does NOT cover.

sections.title: Schedule is part of the source
sections.body: This feed drops nightly before 6:15 AM. Schedules matter because everything downstream inherits them: a late feed is a late brief.

sections.title: Two sources, one case
sections.body: The note said ERCOT hit $187 and settled at $142; this file says the same. The brief cites numbers only when an independent source corroborates the prose - that is why this feed exists in the workflow at all.
